Why are health officials promoting MMR vaccinations? topics: Measles Vaccination MMR Pennsylvania Centre County Pop-up clinics Back-to-school Pharmacies CENTRE COUNTY, Pa (WJAC) — As Measles cases continue to rise statewide, we spoke with health officials in Centre County about what measures healthcare professionals are taking and what they expect to see in the coming weeks. It’s a time that notoriously leads to the spreading of germs as back-to-school season has begun for K-12 and college students. As of Wednesday, the Pennsylvania Department of Health has confirmed two deaths and 423 measles cases across the Commonwealth, including fourteen of those cases in Centre County. The DOH notes that none of these cases have been fully vaccinated individuals. We spoke with Dr. Daniel McKinley of Mount Nittany Health who was able to provide some more information about vaccination options for the public. Powered By 10 Health officials continue to advocate for vaccinations as measles cases rise statewide Share Next Stay He reiterates the message that the best thing you can do to protect yourself and others from measles is to get vaccinated. He says that the vast majority of those who received two doses of the MMR vaccine are protected and do not need a booster. Because of school vaccination requirements, the majority of students in our area have been vaccinated against measles, and because of this, Dr. McKinley says he’s hopeful that back-to-school season will not worsen the spread. He also says that Mount Nittany Health is more than happy to help individuals explore their vaccination options regardless of their beliefs or current vaccination status. “We deal with a whole range of different beliefs and wishes of patients, and our goal is to work with people on what works best for them. And for someone to come in and say I’ve never been vaccinated, that’s not something we’d hold against them in any way, and we’ll be able to talk what their options are, what the risks and benefits are. But I would go ahead and say that the risks of the vaccine are incredibly low.” Mount Nittany and the Department of Health both say that pop up clinics have been assisting in getting people in affected communities vaccinated since late April, and dozens of additional clinics are scheduled for the upcoming weeks. records.content: Health First US measles deaths of 2026 reported. How many cases are in Washington state? By Karlee Van De Venter Don Sweeney , 2 days ago A 3D model shows a visualization of the measles virus. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention/TNS As measles cases increase across the nation, two people have died due to the “highly contagious” disease in Pennsylvania. The two Pennsylvania cases are the first U.S. deaths from measles so far in 2026, health officials said, and the first measles-related fatalities in that state in 35 years. “People are not familiar with this disease and don’t fully understand the potential severity of the illnes s,” Dr. Debra Bogen, Pennsylvania’s ecretary of health, said in a Tuesday, Aug. 25, news release. Neither of the two people who died were vaccinated against the disease, normally considered a childhood illness. This year, Washington state has already reported four times the number of measles cases it logged in 2025. Why are measles cases on the rise in Washington state? Is there an outbreak? Here’s what you should know: What is measles? Where are outbreaks in the U.S.? Measles is a “highly contagious” virus that spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The disease can cause “serious health complications,” especially in children younger than 5 years old, the federal public health agency said. Complications due to measles can include pneumonia, “brain swelling, even blindness and death,” said Dr. Peter Chin-Hong, an infectious disease specialist and professor of medicine at University of California, San Francisco. Measles was considered eliminated in the United States in 2000, the CDC said, meaning that the continuous spread of the disease was stopped for longer than 12 months. What counts as a measles outbreak? The CDC maintains a map tracking measles cases and outbreaks across the country. As of Aug. 20, more than 2,700 confirmed measles cases had been reported by a total of 47 jurisdictions, the CDC said. Two states have reported more than 500 measles cases: Utah and South Carolina. However, a state can have a measles outbreak with far less than 500 cases. According to the CDC, an outbreak is defined as “three or more related cases.” There must be a tie between the cases to be considered an outbreak. “Most outbreaks in the United States are small, comprised of six people or fewer, usually within a household,” the federal health agency said. “When measles gets into a community that has lower vaccination rates it can spread quickly, causing larger outbreaks.” The CDC notes that individual states have the most updated information on outbreaks. How many measles cases does Washington state have? As of Tuesday, there have been 55 confirmed cases of measles in Washington state so far in 2026, according to the state Department of Health. Only four of those 55 cases required hospitalization. No deaths related to Washington measles cases have been reported. Those 50-plus measles cases were spread across eight of Washington’s 39 counties. A third of the cases were reported in Clark County, with 18 total cases. In 2025, only 12 measles cases were reported across Washington state. Why are measles cases increasing in the US? About 90% of unvaccinated people who come in contact with measles get sick with the disease , the California Department of Public Health said. The highly contagious virus can live airborne in a room for up to two hours, the agency said, and it only requires a small amount of particles to infect someone. Measles rates are primarily rising due to high rates of the disease in other parts of the world paired with falling vaccination rates in the United States . Of the 55 cases of measles Washington state has seen in 2026, 89% occurred in individuals confirmed to be unvaccinated. Only one case involved an individual who had two or fewer doses of a measles-containing vaccine, according to the state Department of Health. Five measles cases reported in Washington state in 2026 involved people whose vaccination status is unknown. In other words, none of the cases have involved individuals fully vaccinated against measles. Cuts to public health funding have contributed to measles’ spread, Chin-Hong said, along with a wave of fake conspiracy theories that mislead people about the importance of getting vaccinated. What are common measles symptoms? Measles cases typically start with a high fever, cough, runny nose and watery eyes, according to the CDC. After a few days of symptoms, tiny white spots pop up inside the mouth, the public health agency said, followed by a rash of small red spots that appear on the face and then the rest of the body. Symptoms typically appear about seven to 14 days after being exposed to the virus, the national public health agency said. Here are some of the most common measles symptoms , according to the CDC: High fever Cough Runny nose Red, watery eyes Rash Complications from measles usually include ear infections and diarrhea, while more serious complications include pneumonia and encephalitis. “Some people think of measles as just a little rash and fever that clears up in a few days,” the CDC warned. “But measles can cause serious health complications.” Who is most at risk of measles? “Anyone who is not protected against measles is at risk” of getting sick, according to the CDC. According to the Washington State Department of Health, people at higher risk of measles complications include infants under 12 months old and young children who have not been vaccinated. Unvaccinated pregnant people, their unborn babies and people with weakened immune systems are also more vulnerable, the state health agency said. Due to the highly contagious nature of measles, it is important to limit contact with others, especially those who may not be protected via vaccination, if you develop symptoms. “ Measles spreads easily , and people can pass it on before they realize they’re sick,” said Michele Roberts, the Washington State Department of Health’s assistant secretary for prevention and community health. “We all have busy lives, but if you have symptoms, take a moment to pause — stay home and contact your healthcare provider.” “That simple step can help prevent spreading measles to others,” she added. The state Department of Health recommends calling your doctor or healthcare provider to determine your next steps after identifying symptoms. If you go to a hospital or clinic, it is imperative you call ahead to disclose you want to be checked in for measles. What’s the best way to protect against the virus? “The best way to protect against measles is with the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine ,” the CDC said. The federal health agency said the two-dose vaccine is safe and about 97% effective at preventing measles. Children can be vaccinated against measles as early as 6 months. The CDC recommends that children get one dose between 12 to 15 months, and the second dose at 4 to 6 years old. DALLAS - Dallas County is reporting a confirmed case of the measles and shared three locations where that patient may have exposed others. (Photo by: BSIP/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) What we know: The patient is a Dallas County resident, but no details about his or her identity were shared for privacy reasons. According to the health department, there are three locations where the patient visited last week, possibly exposing others. Turrentine Jackson Morrow Chapel in Allen from 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. on Aug. 14 Gloria’s Restaurant in Fairview from 12:30 p.m. to 5 p.m. on Aug. 14 The Revel Patio Grill in Frisco from around 8 p.m. until midnight on Aug. 15 What they're saying: "Measles is one of the most contagious diseases we know, but it is also highly preventable," said Dr. Philip Huang, the Dallas County health director. "If you were at one of these locations during the identified time period, check your vaccination status and watch closely for symptoms. Most importantly, make sure you and your family are up to date on the MMR vaccine. Vaccination remains our best protection against measles and the best way to prevent further spread in our community." Measles Symptoms Big picture view: Measles is a highly contagious viral illness that spreads through respiratory droplets from an infected person’s cough or sneeze. Symptoms typically start with a high fever, a cough, runny nose, red or watery eyes and white spots inside the mouth. A rash typically develops three to five days after the first symptoms begin. What you can do: Health officials said healthy individuals who are fully vaccinated have a very low risk of contracting the disease. Those who are unvaccinated, too young to be vaccinated or have weakened immune systems should keep an eye out for symptoms and reach out to a healthcare provider with concerns. records.content: 24/7 LivePhiladelphiaPennsylvaniaNew JerseyDelaware 75° Measles Shapiro, Kennedy have war of words following 2 measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania ByBrenda Goodman, Meg Tirrell, CNN Friday, August 28, 2026 1:46PM There's a public health dispute brewing between Pennsylvania and the CDC, concerning the measles outbreak The Pennsylvania Department of Health this week recorded its first two measles-associated deaths in 35 years, both in people who were unvaccinated. The agency declined to provide further details, saying it was protecting patient privacy. What came next was a war of words. Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, said at a news conference Tuesday that he had spoken to US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and "made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America, particularly right here in Pennsylvania." Before becoming HHS secretary under President Trump, Kennedy was a leading voice casting doubt on the safety of vaccination. In 2021, Kennedy - then head of the anti-vaccine organization Children's Health Defense - visited Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, where he made light of his own childhood case of measles and suggested that vaccines were causing autism and autoimmune diseases. On social media Wednesday, Kennedy accused Shapiro of fearmongering and the "weaponization of infectious disease" for political gain. He suggested that the deaths there may have been "altogether fabricated" by one of Shapiro's "hopeful staffers" to support a narrative that measles infection is more dangerous than it actually is. He also said the coroner in Lancaster County, where the two people lived, had no record of any measles-related deaths. Pennsylvania's secretary of health, Dr. Debra Bogen, later weighed in, saying she had thoroughly reviewed the case investigation and "sadly can confirm that there were two recent measles-associated deaths in Lancaster County, which were reported to the CDC's measles response team early Tuesday morning." On Thursday afternoon, however, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in a statement posted to social media that it was working to determine what had actually happened. "These discrepancies raise important questions, particularly because the Governor's Office has not provided CDC with information relevant to the outbreak and has declined our offers of assistance," it said. The Pennsylvania Department of Health fired back. "It is inaccurate to suggest that Pennsylvania has not provided the CDC with information relevant to the outbreak or declined to work with the CDC," it said in a post on social media. The department said it was in touch with the CDC's program staff and regularly shared data with the CDC. Here's what we know about the cases and the conflict. What does 'measles-associated' mean? Deaths are classified as "measles-associated" when lab testing or epidemiological evidence of measles is present but the disease may not be assessed by the medical certifier or coroner to be the immediate cause of death, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health. Bogen said she had thoroughly investigated and verified that both people who died had tested positive for measles. The information was not reported until the results of epidemiological investigations were confirmed, she said. Epidemiologic investigations look at when and where a person got sick and how they may have been exposed to a pathogen. Did measles contribute to the deaths? That's unclear. Lancaster County Coroner Dr. Stephen Diamantoni told reporters Wednesday that his office was reviewing the death of an infant who tested positive for measles. He said the child died shortly after birth from a laceration of the spleen, and measles antibodies were present in postmortem testing. Despite the positive measles test, the forensic pathologist who conducted the autopsy "did not feel it was related to the measles," Diamantoni told the Philadelphia Inquirer. Diamantoni said he has no other cases involving people who tested positive for measles. Kennedy and others have seized on that statement to suggest that if Diamantoni isn't investigating, the other case may not exist at all. The state Department of Health countered that "not all deaths are referred to a coroner under Pennsylvania law." Dr. Adam Ratner, a pediatric infectious disease physician in New York City and author of the 2025 book "Booster Shots: The Urgent Lessons of Measles and the Uncertain Future of Children's Health," said it's premature to assume measles didn't play a role in these deaths. "The problem is that the facts of the cases are not widely known, which is reasonable, because I think that the Pennsylvania public health authorities want to be careful about potentially identifying people," he told CNN. "Calling something a measles-associated death does not mean that the death was not caused by measles. It means that it is entirely possible that that death was caused by measles, and I would say likely," he added. "And the fact of the matter is that we don't see measles-associated deaths when there is not measles circulating in the United States, and there is measles circulating at levels that it has not in decades, as a result of declining confidence of vaccines, largely from the messaging from HHS and elsewhere in the government." How do these cases fit into what's known about measles? Although details on these particular deaths are still sparse, a growing measles outbreak in Pennsylvania fits a predictable pattern. Of the 424 cases reported in Pennsylvania this year - all of them in people who were not fully vaccinated - 73, or about 1 in 6, have involved hospitalization, according to data from the state's Department of Health. Typically during outbreaks, about 1 in 5 unvaccinated people who get sick will be hospitalized, according to the National Foundation for Infectious Diseases. About 1 in 20 children who get measles will get pneumonia, and 1 in 1,000 will develop brain swelling, or encephalitis, which can lead to brain damage. Even with the best care, measles is deadly in about 1 to 3 people out of every 1,000 cases. The two measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania are the first reported this year in the US, where 2,777 cases have been confirmed. The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine confers a high degree of protection. The recommended two doses are about 97% effective at preventing measles, according to the CDC. That's why experts consider deaths from measles to be preventable. The deaths are "tragic," Ratner said. But so too is the effort to try to cast doubt on them, Ratner added. "It's a common anti-vaccine talking point, and it dehumanizes the people who have suffered and died." "We're in a much worse position than we were just a couple years ago in terms of vaccination in general in the United States, and specifically with measles, which we've clearly lost control of." AP Philadelphia: Two unvaccinated Pennsylvania residents have died from measles, the first US deaths this year related to the contagious virus. State health officials announced the deaths Tuesday. They did not reveal any details about the people who died, other than that they lived in Lancaster County, west of Philadelphia. “My deepest sympathies are with the loved ones who are facing this unimaginable loss,” said state Health Secretary Dr. Debra Bogen. “Because measles was largely eliminated in the Commonwealth for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don’t fully understand the potential severity of the illness." Get updated faster and for FREE: Download the Gulf News app now - simply click here. The US has now seen five measles deaths in the last two years — more than the combined total of reported deaths over the previous three decades — and is enduring its worst year for measles since 1991. With 2,777 cases as of Thursday, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, this year already has surpassed 2025's measles count. The US eliminated local measles spread in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, which have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. Governor suggests Trump administration could do more to promote vaccines The measles surge has coincided with moves by President Donald Trump's administration to scale back childhood vaccinations, based on concerns — unfounded, according to scientific studies — about vaccine safety. Trump earlier this month signed an executive order calling for revamped childhood vaccine recommendations. He also advocated separating the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three different shots, and administering all childhood immunizations at separate appointments whenever possible. Also Read: 11 million measles cases expected worldwide in 2026 Doctors have raised concerns that Trump and US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. are stoking confusion and hesitancy. In a media briefing Tuesday, Gov. Josh Shapiro said he had spoken with Kennedy, who offered the assistance of federal health staffers. Shapiro declined the offer, saying Pennsylvania's health department was able to handle the current situation. “I was very, very blunt with him," Shapiro said. "I made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric that’s coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America, particularly right here in Pennsylvania.” He added: "There’s real-life consequences to scaring people and not relying on actual doctors and actual medical professionals to provide unbiased information to parents so that we can make reasonable decisions for our kids." Also Read: Trump signs order calling for spacing out childhood vaccines Federal health officials did not immediately comment on the Pennsylvania deaths or on Shapiro's account of the exchange with Kennedy. Vaccination rates are declining nationwide Decades of widespread vaccinations turned measles cases and deaths into a rarity, causing people to forget that the very contagious virus can be deadly, said Dr. David Margolius, director of Cleveland’s health department and a leader in a coalition of big city health departments. He said that some Cleveland residents have expressed irritation with vaccine-promotion campaigns. “They say, ‘Oh, that’s not a big deal. I mean, do people even die from measles? And, you know, why do you care so much? Why do you keep calling me about this?’” he recounted. Margolius said the Trump administration has reacted to outbreaks with offers of assistance. Also Read: US measles outbreak hits case counts not seen in 35 years “But the time to prevent measles is before the outbreaks happen," he said. "And the way to do that is clear and consistent and very visible messaging" about the importance of vaccinations. The overall U.S. kindergarten vaccination rate inched down last year and the share of children with exemptions rose to an all-time high, according to federal data posted last week. Lancaster County is known as the heart of Pennsylvania's Amish community, a religious group that is sometimes reluctant to embrace modern medical interventions such as vaccines. About 88% of kindergartners in the county were up to date on their measles vaccines during the last school year, according to state data. Pennsylvania has counted nearly 400 measles cases this year, state officials said. The state has been promoting measles vaccinations as cases have risen, and about 35,000 people have been vaccinated, up from the usual pace of about 25,000 per month, officials said. records.content: Latest U.S. Iran War Nepal Flood World Politics Entertainment HealthWatch MoneyWatch Crime Space Sports Brand Studio The Free Press Local News Atlanta Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas Live CBS News 24/7 Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas 48 Hours 60 Minutes Shows 48 Hours 60 Minutes CBS Evening News CBS Mornings CBS Morning News CBS Reports CBS Saturday Morning The Daily Report The Dish Face the Nation Sunday Morning The Takeout Things That Matter The Uplift CBS News Investigates CBS News Confirmed Podcasts Newsletters Download Our App CBS News Team Executive Team Brand Studio Paramount+ Join Our Talent Community RSS Feeds HealthWatch | Diet & Nutrition Fitness Gut Health Self Care Sleep Love & Relationships Watch CBS News HealthWatch As measles outbreaks grow in the U.S., maps and charts show a record number of cases in 2026 By Grace Manthey Grace Manthey Senior Visual Data Journalist, Data Team Coordinator Grace Manthey is the senior visual data journalist and data team coordinator for CBS News and Stations. She is an Emmy-winning journalist and visual storyteller with a passion for telling stories that matter. Read Full Bio Grace Manthey Updated on: August 25, 2026 / 11:25 AM EDT / CBS News Add CBS News on Google So far in 2026, the U.S. has recorded the most measles cases in more than three decades as outbreaks spread in multiple states, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data shows. By mid-July, the number had already surpassed all of 2025, which had been the worst year in recent history with more than 2,200 confirmed cases. Ongoing outbreaks have put the U.S. at risk of losing its official measles elimination status, which it has held since 2000. Pennsylvania's health department announced on Aug. 25 that the state recorded its first two deaths connected to measles in 35 years. The two people who died were not vaccinated against the virus. The deaths occurred in Lancaster County. Measles is one of the most contagious infectious diseases. In some cases, it can cause severe infections in the lungs and brain that can lead to cognitive issues, deafness or death. But it can be prevented by vaccination, which medical research has proven to be safe and highly effective. The CBS News data team has tracked confirmed measles cases nationwide as new data is released by state health departments and the CDC. Out of the 2,289 confirmed cases last year, more than 750 were connected to an outbreak in West Texas that led to the deaths of two children. Prior to 2025, the highest number of confirmed cases in the U.S. in recent years was 1,274 in 2019, driven by outbreaks in New York, California and Washington state. Most years the total was much lower. Health experts point to lower vaccination rates as the main reason for increases in preventable infectious diseases like measles. The vast majority of cases have been in people who were unvaccinated, and outbreaks have spread in communities with lower vaccination rates. CDC data shows about 92.4% of kindergartners in the U.S. got their measles-mumps-rubella shots in the 2025-2026 school year, down slightly from 92.5% the previous year. The figure has declined from 95.2% during the 2019-2020 school year — a critical threshold to keep people safe. Only 10 states hit the 95% threshold last year. "When more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated, most people are protected through community immunity (herd immunity)," the CDC states. In Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, where two measles deaths were reported, the rate was lower: just 87.6% in the latest data. "I think that parents, for most kids, especially for the measles vaccines, the DTP, all the standard childhood vaccines, it's very important that parents vaccinate their kids," Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, the director of the National Institutes of Health, said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan." Research has found no evidence of increased rates of autism among those who are vaccinated compared to those who are not. Vaccines also undergo intensive safety testing. records.content_title: Four measles cases diagnosed in Knox County
records.content: MOUNT VERNON — As of Friday, there have been four measles cases identified in Knox County residents, according to a press release from Knox Public Health. The Ohio Department of Health is working with Knox Public Health (KPH) to follow up on potential exposures and promote opportunities for vaccination. KPH is also working with the individual and their healthcare provider to identify contacts. Knox Public Health will notify the contacts and provide guidance on quarantining. Measles is a highly contagious virus. Individuals infected with measles can spread it to others, even before they have symptoms. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in the air after an infected person leaves the room. Symptoms usually appear 7 to 14 days after a person comes in contact with the virus, but it can take as long as 21 days for symptoms to appear. Measles symptoms include: high fever (may spike from 103° F to 105° F), cough, runny nose, pink/red, watery eyes, and a red/brown blotchy rash. The rash will appear on the face and then spread to the trunk and extremities. Rash and other symptoms usually subside in 7 to 9 days. According to the Ohio Department of Health, about one out of every five people who get measles will be hospitalized. One out of every 1,000 people with measles will develop brain swelling due to infection (encephalitis) which may lead to brain damage. 1 to 3 out of 1,000 people with measles will die, even with the best care. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends all children get two doses of measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, starting with the first dose at 12 through 15 months of age and the second dose at 4 through 6 years of age. Anyone traveling internationally should be fully vaccinated before traveling. Infants 6-11 months old should get one dose of the MMR vaccine before travel, then should receive two additional doses after their first birthday. Older children, adolescents, and adults should receive one or two doses of MMR vaccine if they do not have evidence of immunity. If you have received two doses of the MMR vaccine, your chances of getting measles are very low. After two doses, the vaccine is 97% effective at preventing measles. Talk to your healthcare provider about vaccination if you are unvaccinated or do not know if you are vaccinated. The measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is safe and effective with hundreds of millions of doses given. Please contact your medical provider or Knox County Community Health Center at 740-399-8008 if you have questions about measles, or the MMR vaccination, or would like to schedule a vaccination appointment. If you have symptoms, stay home, avoid contact with others, and call your healthcare provider. Please do not show up in the waiting room without contacting the staff first in case you are contagious. For more information and updates, visit Knox Public Health’s website at: https://www.knoxhealth.com/ index.php . For more information about measles, visit https://www.cdc.gov/measles/

ATLANTA - Four more children have been diagnosed with measles in an outbreak associated with a metro Atlanta daycare, according to the Georgia Department of Public Health. What we know The new cases involve close contacts of a measles case confirmed last week. DPH said the children were either unvaccinated or had not received all recommended doses of the measles vaccine. Advertisement Advertisement Health officials are now working to identify additional people who may have had close contact with the infected children. records.content_title: SSPE: Experts explain rare measles complication, diagnosis and treatment
records.content: Updated On: 25 August, 2026 12:08 PM IST | Mumbai | Vinod Kumar Menon SSPE is a rare neurological complication of measles that can emerge years after infection. Experts explain its diagnosis, treatment challenges and why vaccination is key to prevention Implementing universal measles vaccination could eliminate the threat of SSPE. Representation Pic/iStock Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE) , a rare neurological complication of measles, can emerge years after the initial infection, progressively impairing a child’s brain function, movement, and independence. Despite advances in understanding the disease, it remains without a definitive cure. In part eight of a nine-part series on SSPE, mid-day speaks to medical experts, who shed light on various facets of the condition. Viswanathan LG, Associate Professor of neurology, NIMHANS, Bengaluru, and consultant neurologist and epileptologist, looks at SSPE from the scientific and clinical perspective, explaining the disease process, its biology, diagnosis, and treatment options. NIMHANS receives many cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples from across the country for testing for SSPE. A positive result from NIMHANS provides strong laboratory confirmation of the disease in a patient, who has signs and symptoms consistent with SSPE. Pennsylvania health officials announced today that two residents died from measles, the first such deaths this year in the United States. Two Pennsylvania residents died from measles, health officials said today, the first such deaths this year in the United States, which is contending with the highest number of cases of the highly infectious disease in more than three decades as vaccination rates drop. Both people were unvaccinated residents of Lancaster County, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health, which did not release additional details, citing privacy concerns. Pennsylvania has been one of the hardest hit states this year, with 393 measles cases across 28 counties so far. Lancaster County, in the southeastern part of the state, has had 185 cases, but these were the first measles deaths recorded in the state in 35 years. The United States has had 2,777 confirmed cases so far this year of a disease that had been largely eradicated in the country, a reflection of declining vaccination rates and policies under Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has worked for decades to discourage the use of vaccines. He and President Donald Trump, who earlier this month issued an executive order calling for a reduction in recommended childhood vaccines, have promoted a long-debunked link between vaccines and autism contrary to established scientific evidence. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services was not immediately available for comment. Don't miss out on what's happening! Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE! Email Sign Up By clicking to sign up, you agree to Star-Advertiser's and Google's Terms of Service and Privacy Policy. This form is protected by reCAPTCHA. Vaccination rates of 95% or higher can prevent outbreaks by creating what is known as herd immunity that protects people unable to be vaccinated. Two doses of the Measles-Mumps-Rubella shot provide 97% protection against the virus. Children typically first receive the vaccine when they are 12 to 15 months old and again at age 4 to 6 years of age. According to Pennsylvania Department of Health data for the 2025-2026 school year, 93.2% of Pennsylvania kindergarten-age children had received the required two doses of MMR vaccine, down from 93.7% during the 2024-2025 school year. In Lancaster County, 87.6% of kindergarten students received the required two MMR doses during the 2025-2026 school year. “Because measles was largely eliminated in the Commonwealth for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don’t fully understand the potential severity of the illness,” said Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Debra Bogen. The number of U.S. measles cases in 2026 is the highest in a single year since the major resurgence between 1989 and 1991, when 55,000 infections and 123 deaths were recorded. Videos Celebrity Couples Royals Lifestyle Beauty Fashion Follow Instagram Follow Facebook Like X Follow MAGA Republican Byron Donalds blames illegal immigration for measles outbreak, but his claim quickly falls apart By Wonderwall.com Editors August 25, 2026 Share Article Overview Republican Florida congressman Byron Donalds claimed that "rampant illegal immigration" was driving measles outbreaks across the United States, directly contradicting public health data. The contradiction Donalds made the statement during an August 23 appearance on CBS News' Face the Nation, as host Margaret Brennan pointed out that nearly all of Florida has fallen below the 95% immunization threshold needed for herd immunity against measles. Byron Donalds is running for governor of Florida while serving in Congress. By: MEGA "So, is your message to Florida parents, get your kids vaccinated against that one?” she asked. Instead of answering whether he would advise parents to follow CDC guidance, he responded, "No. Actually, my message to Floridians and, quite frankly, to Americans is, the reason why we have seen a measles outbreak in certain parts of the country is because of rampant illegal immigration into the United States from the previous administration." What the CDC data actually shows The problem with Donalds' claim arose when journalists and health experts examined actual case numbers. According to CDC data as of August 20, only 16 of the nation's 2,777 confirmed measles cases in 2026 came from international visitors, accounting for less than 0.006% of all infections. Meanwhile, 94% of measles cases involved individuals who were either unvaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status. The CDC's research has consistently shown that measles more commonly enters the United States through unvaccinated American residents who contract the virus while traveling abroad and return home. The misinformation problem The U.S. recorded 2,777 confirmed measles cases as of August 20, 2026. Medical professionals and public health experts raised concerns about how political misinformation can fuel vaccine hesitancy at a time when immunity rates are already critically low. Prominent medical expert Dr. George Rust expressed disappointment with Donalds' approach, saying, "We teach our kids not to blame other people for our problems and especially groups of people." Rust emphasized the biological reality underpinning the outbreak: measles is extraordinarily contagious within unvaccinated populations. "If there are 10 unimmunized people in a room and they get exposed to measles, 9 of those 10 are going to get measles," he explained. "It's that infectious." The two-dose MMR vaccine offers 97% protection against measles, while a single dose provides 93% effectiveness according to CDC guidelines. A pattern of blame-shifting Donald Trump has called for changes to how children receive the MMR vaccine. By: MEGA Donalds' approach to the measles question reflected a broader pattern of politicians attributing disease outbreaks to immigration rather than addressing preventable health vulnerabilities. During his appearance, he also mentioned that healthcare costs represented Florida's primary health concern, shifting focus away from vaccination policy entirely. Just months earlier in June 2026, Sen. Roger Marshall blamed President Joe Biden's immigration policies for the spread of screwworm, a flesh-eating parasitic larva that affected livestock. Donald Trump has echoed those sentiments several times in the past. In 2024, he said in an interview with New York radio station WABC, “They’re coming in as terrorists. Many, many terrorists are coming in and people are coming in with very contagious disease." National outbreak context The MMR vaccine protects children against measles, mumps and rubella. As of August 21, 2026, the United States recorded 2,777 confirmed cases, already surpassing the entire 2025 total of 2,289 cases. Forty-eight measles outbreaks were documented in 2025, up from 16 in 2024. By August 2026, 36 outbreaks had been reported just eight months into the year. Vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergarteners dropped from 95.2% during the 2019-2020 school year to 92.4% by 2025-2026, leaving approximately 280,000 kindergarteners vulnerable to infection. Between all this, Trump has also called out the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine as "lethal," claims that Dr. Mehmet Oz has declined. records.content: Latest U.S. Iran War Nepal Flood World Politics Entertainment HealthWatch MoneyWatch Crime Space Sports Brand Studio The Free Press Local News Atlanta Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas Live CBS News 24/7 Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas 48 Hours 60 Minutes Shows 48 Hours 60 Minutes CBS Evening News CBS Mornings CBS Morning News CBS Reports CBS Saturday Morning The Daily Report The Dish Face the Nation Sunday Morning The Takeout Things That Matter The Uplift CBS News Investigates CBS News Confirmed Podcasts Newsletters Download Our App CBS News Team Executive Team Brand Studio Paramount+ Join Our Talent Community RSS Feeds Philadelphia | News Weather Sports Video CBS Philadelphia Shows 75° All News Pennsylvania New Jersey Delaware National World Health Entertainment Politics Traffic & Transportation Business Recalls Latest Weather Radars Closings & Delays All Sports CBS Sports HQ Eagles Sixers Phillies Flyers Blue Coats College High School Odds Focusing on the Future Gallen of Questions Alex's Lemonade Stand Lights for the Fight More Than Pink Friday Football Frenzy Hispanic Heritage Month Joy of Sharing Black Business Month Mental Reset RMHC Telethon Summer Beat Spreading the Love The Heartbeat Station Info Contact Us Share Photos & Video Send Us a News Tip Advertise With Us Contests & Promotions Download The App About NEXTGEN TV Photo Galleries Mentioned On-Air Jobs & Internships Memorials Watch CBS News Local News Pennsylvania health department reports 2 measles deaths in Lancaster County By Joe Brandt Joe Brandt Digital Content Producer, CBS Philadelphia Joe Brandt has been a digital content producer for CBS News Philadelphia since 2022. He is a Temple University graduate and was born and raised in Pitman, NJ. Read Full Bio Joe Brandt Updated on: August 27, 2026 / 10:11 AM EDT / CBS Philadelphia Add CBS News on Google Pennsylvania has recorded its first two deaths connected to measles in 35 years, the state health department announced Tuesday. The two people who died were not vaccinated against the virus, and the deaths occurred in Lancaster County. One of the two deaths, an infant who tested positive for measles, is under investigation by the Lancaster County Coroner's office, the health department said. It is unclear if measles caused the death. Gov. Josh Shapiro and Health Secretary Dr. Debra Bogen held a news conference about the measles deaths on Tuesday morning. So far this year, there have been 393 confirmed cases in 29 counties across the commonwealth. CBS News reports measles cases nationwide are at their highest levels in 35 years. "Because measles was largely eliminated in the Commonwealth for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don't fully understand the potential severity of the illness," Bogen said in a statement. "We want to ensure every Pennsylvanian has the information they need to protect themselves, their loved ones and their communities. As a physician, I want to make sure that people understand that the MMR vaccine is safe and provides the best protection we have against measles." Earlier this month, two measles cases were confirmed in Lehigh County. Protection from measles is included in the shot for measles, mumps and rubella, known as the MMR vaccine, which is typically given to children in two doses, one at 12 to 15 months and another at 4 to 6 years old, according to the CDC. Also in August, President Trump signed an executive order suggesting that the MMR vaccine should be given as three separate shots. The latest figures from the CDC show 92.4% of the nation's kindergarteners have been vaccinated against measles during the 2025-26 school year, down from 95.2% during the 2019-20 school year. A vaccination rate of 95% is needed for herd immunity, CBS News reports. There have been two confirmed deaths from measles in Pennsylvania. Neither victim was vaccinated. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images ) By Bob D'Angelo, Cox Media Group National Content Desk August 26, 2026 at 6:55 am EDT Two unvaccinated people in Pennsylvania have died from measles as a large outbreak continues to spread in the Keystone State, health officials said on Tuesday. The deaths were the first measles-related deaths this year in the United States, The New York Times reported. [ Read more trending news ] Both people who died were residents of Lancaster County, according to The Washington Post. The Pennsylvania Health Department declined to release the victims’ ages or other information, citing their privacy and those of their families, the newspaper reported. “My deepest sympathies are with the loved ones who are facing this unimaginable loss,” state Health Secretary Debra Bogen said in a statement. “Because measles was largely eliminated in the Commonwealth for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don’t fully understand the potential severity of the illness.” Pennsylvania has confirmed 393 measles cases in 28 counties this year, including 86 during the past week, the Post reported. Nearly half of the cases occurred in Lancaster County. According to the Times, 70 people have been hospitalized, and more than a third of the reported cases in the state involved children. Gov. Josh Shapiro said that every confirmed case happened to someone who had not been vaccinated, according to the Post. “We hope and we pray that those deaths will be the last,” Shapiro said during a news conference Tuesday. A case of measles has also been confirmed in western Pennsylvania, WPXI reported. A statement from Michael Fiorina, the chief medical officer at Independence Health System, verified a laboratory-confirmed case of measles in Butler County, according to the television station. In late July, the number of confirmed measles cases in the United States topped the total reported for all of 2025, ABC News reported, citing data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The news outlet reported that last year’s total of 2,289 reported cases of measles was the highest number in more than 30 years. However, the 2,777 cases reported so far this year is the most since 1991, CDC data shows. Two school-aged children and one adult died last year from measles-related complications, the Times reported. They were the first deaths in the U.S. in a decade, according to the newspaper. “These five deaths that have occurred since 2025 are extremely, extremely rare in the modern era,” Amesh Adalja, an infectious disease doctor at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security, told the Times. “They’re also a harbinger of what is happening as this virus takes hold again in the United States.” According to the Mayo Clinic, measles is a contagious, vaccine-preventable disease. Symptoms include fever, cough, congestion and pink eye. Most people recover from measles in about 10 days. “It usually doesn’t cause long-term medical issues. But measles can be serious and even deadly,” the Mayo Clinic noted on its website. “This is especially true for children younger than age 5 and people with severely weakened immune systems. ©2026 Cox Media Group Your browser does not support HTML5 audio. records.content: Skip to main content FactCheck.org® A Project of The Annenberg Public Policy Center FactCheck.org® Home Articles FactCheck Posts SciCheck En Español Players Guide 2026 Project 2025 series Debunking Viral Claims Ask a Question Ask FactCheck Ask SciCheck Donate Topics President Trump Robert F. Kennedy Jr. immigration tariffs inflation climate change coronavirus View All About Us Our Mission Our Process Our Funding Our Staff Undergraduate Fellows Awards Request a Correction Contact Us Search More Viral Claims Newsletter Instagram Threads YouTube TikTok Facebook X FactCheck On the Air What We Know About Pennsylvania’s Two ‘Measles-Associated’ Deaths Kennedy Distorts Stat in Celebrating Obesity Drop Trump’s Misleading Crime Drop Claims Republicans Revive False Miscarriage Statistic, Twist Fauci’s Texts About COVID-19 Shots Trump’s False MMR Vaccine Claims Previous Next What We Know About Pennsylvania’s Two ‘Measles-Associated’ Deaths August 28, 2026 After the Pennsylvania Department of Health announced two cases of measles-related deaths in one county, the local coroner appeared to contradict the account. And in an ongoing spat with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has alleged that a Shapiro staffer may have even “fabricated” the deaths. We’ll lay out what we know. Collins Ad Attacks Jackson on Education Using Questionable U.S. News Ranking for Maine August 28, 2026 A Republican ad attacking Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson in Maine says under his “failed leadership” the state’s high schools “dropped to dead last” in the country, according to annual rankings by U.S. News & World Report. But that’s not the whole story. Ad Attacking Cooper Makes False Connection to Murder August 26, 2026 An ad from a super PAC supporting Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley features a heart-wrenching testimonial from the father of a woman who was murdered in 2025. The ad falsely implies the accused murderer was one of the prisoners released during the COVID-19 pandemic when Whatley’s Democratic opponent, Roy Cooper, was governor of North Carolina. Cooper had nothing to do with the accused murderer’s release. The NRSC’s Weak Ties Between Brown and Deadly Interstate Crash in Ohio August 25, 2026 In the Ohio Senate race, a Republican ad blames former Sen. Sherrod Brown for a deadly crash in April on an Ohio interstate in which an immigrant was charged with vehicular homicide. But there’s no evidence of any tie between Brown’s votes on immigration, as the ad suggests, and the suspect in this incident. Trump’s ‘No Tax on Tips’ Claim Doesn’t Add Up August 25, 2026 The White House has provided no federal data to support President Donald Trump’s claims that because of his “no tax on tips” policy, “440,000 tipped workers” in Nevada “saved an average of $10,000 on their taxes,” and “130,000 tipped workers” in Georgia “saved an average of more than $7,000 on their taxes.” Kennedy Distorts Stat in Celebrating Obesity Drop August 24, 2026 In recent public appearances, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has said obesity dropped 3% “in the last year” and suggested the Trump administration deserves at least some of the credit. One poll shows obesity falling by about that much — but the decline happened over several years and began well before President Donald Trump’s current term. Trump’s Misleading Crime Drop Claims August 20, 2026 In announcing the latest FBI annual report on nationwide crime, President Donald Trump wrongly cast the decline in crime in 2025 as a dramatic turnaround and made misleading claims about the impact of his administration’s policies. RFK Jr. Falsely Claims New Evidence Supports Splitting MMR Vaccine August 18, 2026 Following an executive order that called for breaking up the combination measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said that a “recent” study “just came out” that “very strongly supports” the idea. But there’s no evidence of any such credible study, past or present. Why did Oregon health officials track the Canby Rodeo exposure? topics: Measles Canby Rodeo Oregon Health Authority MMR vaccine Immunity Exposure Symptoms Public health PORTLAND, Ore. (KATU) — Oregon health officials are tracking a recent measles exposure at the Canby Rodeo earlier this month. The Oregon Health Authority said anyone at the Canby Rodeo on August 18 between 7:30 and 11 p.m. may have been exposed someone with measles. State health officials say people should check their vaccination records and watch for symptoms, and if you aren’t immune they urge you to get an MMR vaccine as soon as possible. They say measles typically starts with a fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes. That is usually followed by a rash that starts on the face and spreads to the rest of the body. The symptoms can start between a week and three weeks after exposure. Powered By 10 Sec Rep. Bonamici speaks out against Trump administration Head Start proposals Next Stay 5 “Common complications of measles include ear infection, lung infection and diarrhea. Swelling of the brain is a rare but much more serious complication,” the OHA said. “Measles can be dangerous, especially among infants and children younger than 5 years old, adults older than 20 years, pregnant people, and people with weakened immune systems.” If you think you or someone in your house may have measles, call your doctor ahead of time before showing up at a medical office to limit exposure to others. You should call your doctor if you have a measles-like rash, or have other symptoms and have also been exposed in the last 21 days. records.content: 24/7 LiveNew York CityNew JerseyLong IslandNorthern SuburbsConnecticut 73° Measles Baby among 2 unvaccinated measles deaths in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania Thursday, August 27, 2026 1:30PM Pennsylvania officials say an infant was among the two unvaccinated patients who died while being infected with measles. LANCASTER COUNTY, Pa. -- Pennsylvania officials say an infant was among the two unvaccinated patients who died while infected with measles. These are the first deaths related to measles within the state in 35 years, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health, and the first deaths reported this year in the U.S. Both deadly cases were in Lancaster County, about an hour west of Philadelphia. In late July, the number of confirmed measles cases in the U.S. surpassed the total reported for all of last year, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Last year's total of 2,289 was the highest number of recorded measles cases in more than 30 years, CDC data shows. However, the 2,777 total marks the highest number of cases recorded since 1991. There has been a public war of words between Gov. Josh Shapiro's administration and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. about whether these patients actually died of complications from measles or other causes. The CDC currently recommends that people receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at ages 12 to 15 months and the second between 4 and 6 years old. One dose is 93% effective and two doses are 97% effective against measles, the CDC says. Report a correction or typo Copyright © 2026 WPVI-TV. All Rights Reserved. records.content: Home / Mumbai / Mumbai News / Article / Rare measles complication SSPE: Experts discuss diagnosis, treatment and prevention Rare measles complication SSPE: Experts discuss diagnosis, treatment and prevention Updated On: 25 August, 2026 12:08 PM IST | Mumbai | Vinod Kumar Menon SSPE is a rare neurological complication of measles that can emerge years after infection. Experts explain its diagnosis, treatment challenges and why vaccination is key to prevention Listen to this article : Implementing universal measles vaccination could eliminate the threat of SSPE. Representation Pic/iStock Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE) , a rare neurological complication of measles, can emerge years after the initial infection, progressively impairing a child’s brain function, movement, and independence. Despite advances in understanding the disease, it remains without a definitive cure. In part eight of a nine-part series on SSPE, mid-day speaks to medical experts, who shed light on various facets of the condition. Understanding the disease Viswanathan LG, Associate Professor of neurology, NIMHANS, Bengaluru, and consultant neurologist and epileptologist, looks at SSPE from the scientific and clinical perspective, explaining the disease process, its biology, diagnosis, and treatment options. NIMHANS receives many cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples from across the country for testing for SSPE. A positive result from NIMHANS provides strong laboratory confirmation of the disease in a patient, who has signs and symptoms consistent with SSPE. records.content: Home / Mumbai / Mumbai News / Article / Mid-Day Special: Dr T Jacob John on early diagnosis, measles prevention and misdiagnosis Mid-Day Special: Dr T Jacob John on early diagnosis, measles prevention and misdiagnosis Updated On: 26 August, 2026 08:51 AM IST | Mumbai | Vinod Kumar Menon Dr T Jacob John, a pioneer in clinical virology in India, explains the early warning signs of SSPE, why developmental regression and seizures in children should prompt testing, and how measles prevention, vaccination and stronger public-health systems can help reduce the disease Listen to this article : Dr T Jacob John, former professor and head of clinical virology and microbiology at Christian Medical College, Vellore, Tamil Nadu. Pic/By Special Arrangement Dr T Jacob John is a globally recognised virologist and paediatric infectious-disease specialist whose pioneering work in clinical virology has significantly shaped infectious-disease research and prevention in India. A former professor and head of clinical virology and microbiology at Christian Medical College, Vellore, Tamil Nadu, he established India’s first diagnostic virology laboratory and made landmark contributions to the understanding of polio, measles, HIV, and other viral diseases. His work with colleagues also helped document the high incidence of Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE) in South India. records.content_title: When measles returns: The rare brain disease that can emerge years after infection
records.content: Updated On: 23 August, 2026 10:29 PM IST | Mumbai | Vinod Kumar Menon Years after a child appears to recover from the virus, a mutated remnant can persist in the brain, triggering a relentless loss of memory, movement, speech and independence SSPE is a rare, progressive, usually fatal neurological disease caused by persistent measles infection. (Pics/ Special Arrangement) A child recovers from measles . The fever disappears, the rash fades, and the family believes the illness is over. Years later, however, the child may begin forgetting lessons, losing previously acquired skills or behaving differently. School performance deteriorates. Falls become frequent. Then come sudden jerking movements, seizures and progressive loss of movement, speech and vision. In severe cases, the child can eventually lose the ability to walk, swallow, communicate or remain conscious. This is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a rare, progressive and usually fatal neurological disease caused by persistent, altered measles virus infection in the brain.
